title: The Ski Trip You Already Paid For
text:
In the early 1980s, Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer of Ohio University studied why people keep investing in something because they have already paid for it.

In one questionnaire, students imagined they had bought a 100-dollar ticket for a weekend ski trip to Michigan and, later, a 50-dollar ticket for a trip to Wisconsin that they expected to enjoy more. Then they discovered both trips fell on the same weekend, and neither ticket could be sold or refunded. Which would they go on? More than half chose Michigan, the more expensive trip they expected to enjoy less. The money was gone either way, yet the larger sunk cost pulled them toward the worse weekend.

Arkes and Blumer then tested the idea in a real setting. People buying season tickets for the Ohio University theater were randomly sold them at full price or at one of two discounts. The researchers tracked attendance using the stubs. During the first half of the season, those who had paid full price attended more plays than those who had received a discount. Having paid more made people feel they had to get their money's worth, although the money spent could not be recovered either way. The difference faded later in the season.

The authors described this as the sunk cost effect: a tendency to continue an endeavor once money, effort or time has been invested, even when only future costs and benefits should matter.
lesson: When deciding whether to continue a project, course or purchase, ignore what you have already spent. Ask only which choice gives the best future from where you stand now.
source: Arkes, H. R., and Blumer, C. (1985). The psychology of sunk cost. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 35(1), 124-140.
